Guide / November 2026

How to get commercial work as a contractor, without getting burned.

To get commercial work as a contractor, start small and local: property managers, facilities managers, shop and office owners, and builders who need a reliable trade. Have your insurance certificate, licence and safety paperwork ready to send the same day, show photos of similar work, and answer fast. Before you sign anything, check the payment terms, because commercial clients often pay monthly, 30 days or more after the invoice, and may hold back a retention.

How do you get commercial work as a contractor?

Most trades who make the jump do it the same way. They do not start with a big tender. They start with small, repeat jobs for people who look after buildings, and they grow from there:

  1. Pick a lane. Light commercial work close to what you already do: shop fitouts, office repairs, maintenance for rental blocks, small warehouses. A residential electrician can do lighting upgrades in shops long before wiring a new hospital.
  2. Get your paperwork ready. Commercial clients check insurance and safety documents before they check your price. If you cannot send them the same day, you are out.
  3. Find the people who hold the work. Property managers, facilities managers, building owners, strata or HOA managers, and main contractors.
  4. Ask for a small job first. One reactive callout done well gets you on the approved list. The list is where the steady work lives.
  5. Run the cash flow sum before you say yes, so a slow payer cannot sink you.

Owners in trade forums say much the same. The ones who landed a first contract talk about walking into local businesses and property management offices with a card and proof of insurance, sending before and after photos, and having their insurance certificate and tax form ready to email straight away. The common thread is direct contact with the people who look after buildings, not paid lead apps.

Who actually hands out commercial work?

WhoWhat they needHow to reach them
Property managersRepairs, turnovers between tenants, urgent calloutsVisit or email their office; ask who manages vendors
Facilities managersPlanned maintenance, small projects, out of hours workLinkedIn, the reception desk at business parks, referrals from other trades on site
Strata, body corporate or HOA managersCommon area repairs, roofs, paths, lightingTheir management company; many keep an approved list
Shop, office and restaurant ownersFitouts, repairs, quick fixes outside opening hoursWalk in during quiet hours; local business groups
Main contractors and buildersReliable subcontractors who turn up and finishCall their estimator or project manager; ask to join their bid list
Councils and governmentMaintenance and minor works, often through frameworksOfficial tender portals (see below)

For most small firms, property managers are the best first target. They need trades every week, they hate chasing unreliable ones, and one good manager can look after dozens of buildings.

What paperwork do commercial clients ask for?

Expect a vendor pack or a prequalification form. Insurers who help contractors with property manager requirements list the usual items: general liability (public liability outside the USA), workers' compensation where you have staff, commercial vehicle cover, sometimes umbrella or professional cover, plus endorsements naming the client as an additional insured and a waiver of subrogation when the contract asks for them, and an active business licence where one applies. The limits vary by client, so ask for their exact requirements before you call your broker.

What each country tends to add:

  • USA: a certificate of insurance (COI) and a Form W-9. Larger clients may ask for an OSHA 10 or 30 card, a safety record or a bond on bigger jobs. Federal work starts with registering on SAM.gov.
  • UK: public liability and employer's liability insurance, risk assessments and method statements (RAMS), and often a health and safety accreditation. CHAS, SafeContractor and Constructionline are the common ones. CHAS lists memberships from £429 a year on its own site, and the others charge annual fees too, so check which one your target clients actually ask for before you pay for any.
  • Canada: proof of liability insurance and a workers' compensation clearance letter or certificate from your province (WSIB in Ontario, WCB in many others). Some clients ask for a COR safety certificate. Public work is listed on CanadaBuys and provincial portals.
  • Australia: public liability cover, a White Card for construction sites, and Safe Work Method Statements (SWMS) for high risk work. Federal tenders are on AusTender, and each state has its own portal.
  • New Zealand: public liability cover, a health and safety plan, and often a Site Safe passport for site work. Government tenders are on GETS.

Put all of it in one folder as PDFs, named clearly, so you can reply to a vendor form within the hour. Being quick with paperwork is one of the easiest ways to stand out to a busy manager.

What should you say to a property manager?

Keep it short. They get a lot of emails. Copy this and change the details:

"Subject: Reliable [trade] for your buildings in [area]

Hi [name], I run [business], a [trade] business based in [town]. We look after [type of work, such as repairs, turnovers and urgent callouts] for homes and small commercial buildings across [area]. We are fully insured and can send our certificate, licence and safety documents today. We answer the phone during the day and reply within an hour. If you have a job that is waiting for a trade, or need a backup when your usual one is busy, I would be glad to take it on. Photos of recent jobs: [link to your website]. Thanks, [name, phone]."

If you walk in instead, ask for the person who manages vendors, leave a card and a single sheet, and say: "We are a local [trade] business. If you ever need someone at short notice, we turn up and we send the paperwork the same day. Could I email you our insurance certificate?" Then email it that afternoon.

Follow up once after a week and again after a month. A useful line: "Just checking you have our details on file for the next time a [trade] job comes up."

What is a capability statement and do you need one?

A capability statement is a single page that tells a commercial client what you do and why you are safe to hire. Larger clients and government buyers often ask for one. Include:

  • Business name, contact details, licence and registration numbers
  • The services you offer and the areas you cover
  • Three to five similar jobs with a photo each
  • Insurance types and limits, safety accreditations and tickets
  • Your response times and out of hours availability

Your website should say the same thing. A commercial buyer who searches your name wants to see a commercial services page, photos of that kind of work and a clear phone number. If yours only shows kitchens, see what a trade website needs.

How does commercial payment work, and can you afford it?

This is where trades get hurt. Residential customers usually pay a deposit and pay on completion. Commercial clients often pay monthly against progress, 30 days or more after your invoice, and many hold back a retention (called retainage in the USA). A 2026 guide to US retainage notes the holdback is often 5% or 10%, and many states cap it, sometimes at 5% on public work. Retention exists in the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand too, with different rules.

Here is a worked example for a $40,000 job over two months, with monthly invoices, payment 30 days after each invoice and a 10% retention:

WhenWhat happensCash in
Month 1You do $20,000 of work, paying wages and materials as you go$0
End of month 1You invoice $20,000; 10% retention ($2,000) is held$0
Month 2You do the other $20,000 of work; first payment arrives late in the month$18,000
End of month 2Final invoice $20,000; another $2,000 held$0
Month 3Second payment arrives$18,000
After sign offRetention of $4,000 released, often weeks or months later$4,000

So you carry roughly a month or two of costs yourself before money arrives. If wages and materials run at $15,000 a month, you need that much cash or credit on hand before you start. If you do not have it, take a smaller job first, negotiate a materials deposit, or ask for fortnightly billing. Our guides on getting paid on time and pricing a job help with the rest.

Read the contract for three things before you sign: when you are paid (and whether it is "pay when paid"), how much retention is held and when it comes back, and whether there are penalties for finishing late. If any of it is unclear, ask an adviser.

Should you bid on public tenders?

Sometimes, but rarely first. Tenders take hours to write and the competition is wide. They suit firms that already have commercial references, insurance at the required level and someone who enjoys paperwork. If you want to look, start with the official portals: SAM.gov in the USA, Find a Tender in the UK, CanadaBuys in Canada, AusTender in Australia and GETS in New Zealand, plus your local council or state portal for smaller maintenance work. Many councils run frameworks or approved lists for minor works, which suit small trades better than one off tenders.

A faster route for most trades is to subcontract to the firms that win those tenders. Look at who won recent local contracts, then call them and ask to join their supplier list.

How do you keep commercial clients once you have them?

Commercial work is won on price once and kept on reliability forever. What managers value most:

  • Answering the phone and confirming a time the same day.
  • Turning up when you said, signing in, and leaving the site clean.
  • Photos before and after sent with every invoice, so the manager can show the owner what was done.
  • Invoices that match their system: the purchase order number, the site address and the job reference every time.
  • Telling them early when something will cost more, in writing, before you do it.

Do that for three or four jobs and you usually become their first call. Then ask: "Do you manage any other buildings where we could help?" That one question builds more commercial work than any advert. And because word spreads between managers, a profile with good reviews helps too. See how trades get found on Google.

Do this now

Your checklist.

  1. 01Choose one type of light commercial work close to what you already do
  2. 02Ask your broker for a certificate of insurance and check your cover limits
  3. 03Make a folder of insurance, licence, safety and tax documents as PDFs
  4. 04Write a one page capability statement with photos of similar jobs
  5. 05Add a commercial services page with photos to your website
  6. 06Email or visit five property or facilities managers this month
  7. 07Run the cash flow sum before you accept monthly or 30 day terms
  8. 08Send photos and the purchase order number with every invoice
Quick answers

Common questions.

How do I get my first commercial contract?

Start with small reactive jobs for property managers, facilities managers and local businesses. Have your insurance certificate and safety documents ready to send the same day, do the first job well, and ask to go on their approved vendor list.

What insurance do I need for commercial work?

Usually general or public liability insurance, workers' compensation or employer's liability if you have staff, and vehicle cover. Many clients also want to be named as an additional insured. Ask each client for their exact limits before you speak to your broker.

Is commercial work more profitable than residential?

It can be steadier, with bigger and repeat jobs, but margins are often tighter and payment is slower. Many trades keep a mix of both so a slow paying commercial client never leaves them short.

How long do commercial clients take to pay?

Payment terms of 30 days or more after invoice are common, often with monthly progress billing and a retention held until the work is finished. Agree the terms in writing before you start.

Do I need CHAS or Constructionline to get commercial work in the UK?

Not always, but many principal contractors, councils, housing associations and facilities firms ask for a health and safety accreditation. Find out which scheme your target clients accept before paying for one.

How do I find commercial jobs to bid on?

Ask property managers and builders to add you to their bid or vendor lists, and check official tender portals such as SAM.gov, Find a Tender, CanadaBuys, AusTender and GETS, plus your local council.
